# Cathode-ray tube and television (`television_crt`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs vacuum_tube; helped by electromagnetic_waves_radio, photography, atomic_structure
- Core idea: In an evacuated glass tube a beam of electrons from a hot cathode is focused on a screen coated with a phosphor, which glows where it is struck; electric plates or magnetic coils steer the beam. Driven by a steadily rising voltage it draws the changing voltage of a signal as a curve (oscilloscope), the basic measuring instrument of electronics. For television the picture is cut into several hundred horizontal lines scanned 25 or 30 times a second; the brightness along each line is sent as a varying signal, and in the receiver a beam sweeping in exact step paints it on the screen while its strength follows the signal. The eye fuses the lines and frames into a moving picture.
- Pitfalls:
  - Trying to send the whole picture at once over many wires; the key is scanning point by point over one channel, faster than the eye can follow
  - Losing synchronisation between camera and receiver; synchronising pulses must be sent with every line and frame
  - Underrating the bandwidth: a picture needs hundreds of times the frequency band of speech, hence very short waves
  - High voltage on the tube: thousands of volts, a risk of implosion and, at higher voltages, X-rays
- History: europe: 1884 – Nipkow's scanning disc patent (Berlin); 1897 Braun's cathode-ray tube (Strasbourg); 1907–1911 Rosing (St Petersburg) and Campbell Swinton propose cathode-ray television; 1925–1926 Baird shows mechanical television (London); 1935–1936 regular services in Berlin and London; east_asia: December 1926 – Takayanagi (Hamamatsu) shows a character scanned by a Nipkow disc on a cathode-ray tube receiver; americas: 1923 – Zworykin applies for a patent on a camera tube, working iconoscope by 1931–1933; 1927 Farnsworth transmits the first all-electronic image (San Francisco)
- Read:
  - Albert Abramson, The History of Television, 1880 to 1941 (1987)
